'''Dieter Oesterhelt''' (10 November 1940 – 28 November 2022)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hegemann |first1=Peter |last2=Michel |first2=Hartmut |date=2023-01-27 |title=Dieter Oesterhelt (1940–2022) |journal=Science |language=en |volume=379 |issue=6630 |pages=337 |doi=10.1126/science.adg5458 |pmid=36701443 |bibcode=2023Sci...379..337H |s2cid=256275449 |issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free }}</ref> was a German biochemist. From 1980 until 2008, he was director of the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]], Martinsried.

==Biography==
Oesterhelt studied chemistry at [[LMU Munich]] from 1959 to 1963. From 1964 to 1967, he worked at the Institute of Biochemistry at the same university under [[Feodor Lynen]]. He was then a research assistant at the Max Planck Institute for Cell Chemistry until 1969. From 1969 to 1973, he worked as an academic adviser at the Institute for Biochemistry at LMU Munich and carried out work on the structure, function and biosynthesis of the purple membrane of [[Halobacterium salinarum]]. In 1975, he became a junior research group leader at the [[Friedrich Miescher Laboratory of the Max Planck Society|Friedrich Miescher Laboratory]] in Tübingen. From 1976 to 1979, he was a full professor at the [[University of Würzburg]]. Oesterhelt has been a member of the [[Max Planck Society]] and director of the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Martinsried, since 1980. He retired in 2008.<ref name="Henning 2011 p. ">{{cite book | last=Henning | first=Eckart | title=Chronik der Kaiser-Wilhelm-, Max-Planck-Gesellschaft zur Förderung der Wissenschaften 1911 – 2011; Daten und Quellen | publisher=Duncker & Humblot | publication-place=Berlin | year=2011 | isbn=978-3-428-13623-0 | oclc=734081095 | language=de | page=}}</ref><ref>[https://www.biochem.mpg.de/2284/suchergebnis?utf8=%E2%9C%93&searchfield=oesterhelt Various articles about Oesterhelt]</ref>

In 1969, Oesterhelt went to the University of California at [[University of California, San Francisco|San Francisco]], where he joined the lab of Walther Stoeckenius to study the cell membrane of [[Halobacterium|Halobacterium salinarum]]. He proved that retinaldehyde was contained in a protein of the so-called "purple membrane" of Halobacterium. This protein was isolated and called [[bacteriorhodopsin]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Oesterhelt|first1=Dieter|last2=Stoeckenius|first2=Walther|date=September 1971|title=Rhodopsin-like Protein from the Purple Membrane of Halobacterium halobium|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/newbio233149a0|journal=Nature New Biology|language=en|volume=233|issue=39|pages=149–152|doi=10.1038/newbio233149a0|pmid=4940442|issn=2058-1092|url-access=subscription}}</ref> After returned to Germany, Oesterhelt showed that  physiological function of bacteriorhodopsin is to pump protons out of the cell.<ref name="Oesterhelt Stoeckenius pp. 2853–2857">{{cite journal | last1=Oesterhelt | first1=D. | last2=Stoeckenius | first2=W. | title=Functions of a New Photoreceptor Membrane | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=70 | issue=10 | date=1 October 1973 | issn=0027-8424 | doi=10.1073/pnas.70.10.2853 | pages=2853–2857| pmid=4517939 | pmc=427124 | bibcode=1973PNAS...70.2853O | doi-access=free }}</ref> Members of his department at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry researched the structure-function relationships of membrane proteins and other microbial rhodopsins such as [[halorhodopsin]], which later became a molecular tool in [[optogenetics]]. In 2021, he received the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]].<ref>[https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/light-sensitive-microbial-proteins-optogenetics/ Lasker Awards].</ref>

Oesterhelt died on 28 November 2022, at the age of 82.<ref>{{cite web |title=Prof. Dr. Dieter Oesterhelt († 28. November 2022) |url=https://www.mpg.de/17580753/lasker-preis |website=MPG |access-date=30 November 2022}}</ref>
